title: Deliver programmable genome editors selectively to diverse cells in the body

concept.text: The innovation would be an adaptable way to carry programmable genome editors into chosen cell types across multiple organs of a living body. An editor specifies the intended genetic change; the delivery system must bring the editing machinery to enough intended cells for that change to occur while limiting exposure and editing elsewhere. The proposed advance is the ability to adapt delivery across diverse, difficult-to-reach targets, beyond isolated successes with particular tissues.

Selectivity has several distinct meanings that must be evaluated separately: where the delivery vehicle and editor physically travel, where the editor is expressed or becomes active, which cells undergo editing, and what biological effects follow. Restricted expression or editing does not by itself prove restricted physical delivery. A useful platform would therefore combine adaptable targeting with measurements that distinguish these stages.

significance.text: If achieved, adaptable delivery would remove a major constraint on where existing programmable editors can be used. The direct consequence would be access to cell populations and biological settings that current delivery approaches reach inadequately. Its revolutionary potential lies in making targeting more reusable: editors and disease targets could potentially be exchanged within a versatile delivery framework, reducing the need to develop an entirely separate approach for every application.

Broader delivery could expand the range of diseases investigated and eventually treated through genome editing, but delivery success would establish only part of the therapeutic case. Each application would still need evidence that the chosen edit produces the intended benefit, reaches enough relevant cells, lasts sufficiently long and has acceptable safety. The importance of target-cell coverage would depend on the disease and the biological effect being sought; reaching several organs would not establish that every disease in those organs is treatable.

Synthesis: The useful platform analogy is a reusable means of connecting an editor to a cellular target. Its limit is biological heterogeneity: tissues differ in accessibility, immune interactions and intracellular handling. Even a major delivery advance could require target-specific formulations, routes or dosing, and would not automatically confer universal access or predictable clinical outcomes.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is adaptable, sufficiently selective delivery across difficult cell types in multiple organs. Anatomical barriers constrain which tissues an administration route can reach, and molecular targeting cannot be assumed to overcome an inaccessible route. Local administration can improve access to a particular location, but such success does not establish that the same approach can reach dispersed targets elsewhere in the body.

After reaching a tissue, delivery must also succeed at the cellular level. Differences among cell types in how they take up and process delivery systems can prevent a method that works in one population from transferring to another. Broad biodistribution, toxicity and immune responses create additional constraints: increasing exposure to improve target-cell coverage may also increase exposure elsewhere. Repeat administration adds a further challenge because immune and tolerability limits can restrict whether an effective delivery method can be used again.

A related measurement barrier is establishing why a delivery strategy appears selective. Physical accumulation, editor expression and editing outcomes can differ, so an editing result alone cannot resolve the distribution of editor and vehicle components. The supplied review calls for tracking these components over multiple time points. Such measurements are needed to distinguish successful targeting from restricted activity after wider exposure and to interpret safety alongside efficacy.

current_state.text: Ngo, Wu, Wasko and Doudna’s review, “Targeted delivery of genome editors in vivo,” DOI 10.1038/s41587-025-02945-w, describes clinical and preclinical progress in delivery, including liver-directed clinical editing. It also discusses liver accumulation after intravenous dosing, limitations of alternative administration routes and continuing difficulty targeting tissues and cells outside the liver. These achievements establish progress in particular settings; the supplied review does not present a demonstration of the adaptable, multi-organ capability defined here.

The review’s vision of versatile platforms with interchangeable editors and targets is a future direction. An improved editor, a successful delivery vehicle for one tissue, or separate successes in different organs would not alone demonstrate that targeting can be adapted reproducibly across difficult cell types. The supplied evidence summary provides no quantitative coverage, selectivity or safety results sufficient to assess such a platform against the proposed completion criteria.

The exact publication date remains unresolved. Earlier material assigned January 12, 2026, but the supplied review reports that the retained PDF contains an unspecified online-publication date. Its 2026 copyright notice does not establish that exact date. No freshness search record was supplied to establish whether subsequent work had achieved the proposed capability by November 1, 2026. The evidence therefore supports the technical challenge described in the review, without establishing continued nonachievement through that date.

The supplied evidence review reports a complete text extraction of the retained PDF through its references and end matter, without reported truncation or extraction problems. Its assessment did not depend on inspecting figure graphics. The account here relies on that supplied review and its reported passages; the underlying primary studies were not independently inspected. This limits the granularity of claims about individual demonstrations without negating the progress summarized by the review.

completion_criteria.text: Proposal: Demonstrate an adaptable delivery approach for specified programmable editors in several difficult-to-reach cell types across different organs of a relevant mammalian model. Define the target populations, administration routes, doses and success thresholds before testing, including minimum target-cell coverage and acceptable exposure and editing in unintended cells. Show how the approach is adapted between targets so that the evidence tests platform adaptability. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposal

completion_criteria.text: Proposal: Measure the physical biodistribution of both editor and delivery-vehicle components across multiple time points, separately from editor expression, intended editing and phenotypic effects. Quantify target-cell coverage, intended edit outcomes, bystander changes, off-target editing and editing in unintended cell populations. Distinguish an unintended genetic change within a target cell from an intended edit occurring in the wrong cell type, since these represent different failures.
completion_criteria.label: Proposal

completion_criteria.text: Proposal: Establish durability, tolerability and reproducibility under predefined conditions, including at least one application that requires repeat administration. Independent replication should reproduce the claimed delivery and editing performance, with enough detail to assess the adaptations required for each target. Report practical boundaries such as dose limits, inaccessible cell populations and conditions under which selectivity or repeat dosing fails.
completion_criteria.label: Proposal

completion_criteria.text: Proposal: Treat successful mammalian experiments as evidence of demonstrated breadth within the tested targets and conditions. Finite tests cannot establish literal universality. Human delivery, disease-specific clinical benefit and long-term human safety would require separate demonstrations; they should not be inferred from completion of the mammalian milestone.
completion_criteria.label: Proposal

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BIO-03, “Predict the effects of genome changes across biological contexts,” addresses what an edit will do, whereas BIO-15 addresses getting the editing machinery into selected cells. BIO-04, “Create an experimentally predictive virtual cell,” could help predict cellular responses to editing or delivery, but predictive modeling would require experimental delivery validation. BIO-14, “Establish causal functions for noncoding elements and poorly understood proteins,” could benefit from selective editing as a perturbation tool; establishing biological function remains a separate explanatory achievement.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-06, “Enable complete, patterned regeneration of complex mammalian structures,” and BIO-07, “Reversibly restore youthful function across an aged organism,” could potentially use selective genome editing as one intervention. Neither regeneration nor rejuvenation follows automatically from reaching the relevant cells: both require appropriate biological programs, coordinated responses and functional outcomes. BIO-15 would supply an enabling capability rather than establish either result.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-09, “Observe and causally test whole-brain computation at cellular resolution,” and BIO-13, “Establish the physical mechanisms that store and retrieve a long-term memory,” could overlap with selective editing when causal experiments require perturbing defined neural populations. Delivering an editor does not itself provide whole-brain observation or explain memory storage. BIO-10, “Observe molecular state and dynamics inside living cells at scale,” has a complementary measurement role: observing delivery and cellular responses is distinct from controlling where editing occurs.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-05, “Design functional enzymes to specification across reaction classes,” overlaps through the possibility of designing editor proteins, but enzyme function and in-body delivery are separate engineering problems. BIO-08, “Make major cereal crops reliably obtain most of their nitrogen biologically,” may involve genome engineering, yet its plant and ecological requirements differ from this proposal’s mammalian delivery milestone.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-01, “Build an autonomously reproducing cell from defined components,” concerns constructing a cellular system rather than delivering editors into an existing body. BIO-02, “Demonstrate a plausible chemical transition from nonlife to evolution,” BIO-11, “Reconstruct the major steps in the origin of eukaryotic cells,” and BIO-12, “Explain how biological homochirality could emerge and persist,” concern biological origins. They share a broad connection to understanding and engineering living systems, but none is a prerequisite or completion test for BIO-15.

change_log.change: Preserved BIO-15 and its title while expanding the explanation of adaptable delivery across multiple organs and difficult cell types.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent and useful; uncertainty about a supporting date or later developments does not justify removing or redefining it.

change_log.change: Separated physical delivery, editor expression or activity, editing outcomes and phenotypic effects throughout the record.
change_log.reason: The validated review identifies these as distinct measurements and warns that restricted expression or editing cannot establish restricted physical biodistribution.

change_log.change: Replaced the asserted January 12, 2026 publication date with an explicit unresolved date.
change_log.reason: The retained PDF reportedly contains an online-publication placeholder, so the exact date is not verified by its content.

change_log.change: Qualified the claim that the proposed capability remains unestablished through November 1, 2026.
change_log.reason: The supplied review does not demonstrate the capability, but the absent freshness search record cannot establish that no subsequent achievement occurred.

change_log.change: Expanded the completion proposal to include predefined thresholds, component-level biodistribution over time, independent replication and practical failure boundaries.
change_log.reason: These additions make the proposed milestone more assessable while preserving its status as a proposal rather than a source-prescribed standard.

change_log.change: Integrated route accessibility, cell-dependent processing, immune constraints and repeat-administration challenges into the missing breakthrough.
change_log.reason: These useful scientific distinctions explain why isolated tissue successes do not establish adaptable delivery.

change_log.change: Retained conditional therapeutic significance and distinguished mammalian delivery demonstrations from human translation.
change_log.reason: Delivery success does not establish disease-specific benefit, durability or acceptable clinical safety.

change_log.change: Added roster-based relationships and stated the limits of the supplied evidence inspection.
change_log.reason: The final record should explain conceptual connections without merging entries and should not imply independent inspection of primary studies or figure graphics.

unresolved_issues: The exact online publication date of the retained review is unresolved; January 12, 2026 is not verified by the supplied content.
No supplied freshness search establishes the capability’s achievement or nonachievement through November 1, 2026.
The supplied evidence summary does not provide quantitative results from individual primary studies sufficient to assess a platform against the proposed completion criteria.
Specific target cells, organs, editors, mammalian models and numerical success thresholds remain to be selected for a convincing demonstration.
How much target-specific modification a delivery system can require while still demonstrating useful platform adaptability remains to be defined.
Human applicability, disease-specific benefit, long-term safety and feasible repeat administration would remain separate empirical questions after a successful mammalian demonstration.
